extracted.intended_audience: academic authors and referees in computer science / mathematical writing (students, journal referees, conference reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for referees and authors on judging publishability, preparing referee reports, and producing clear mathematical/computer-science papers and illustrations. Emphasis on constructive refereeing, clarity of exposition, good use of diagrams, and notational simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication decision categories (1–4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers generally fall into four categories: (1) Publish essentially as is; (2) Publish after author's minor revision (referee suggests points which must be changed before publication); (3) Publish only if the author makes major revisions (revised paper will be refereed again); (4) Reject (nothing salvageable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only put a paper in category 1 if its substance is significant enough to warrant the editorial effort; avoid over-generous category-1 placements. If placed into category 3, indicate required major revisions and note that the paper will be refereed again.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee's primary goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the quality of publication as high as possible and help the author produce better papers in the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the referee's report to give the author maximum benefit while not compromising on quality. Aim to get every author to produce the best paper he/she is capable of writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contribution / significance
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper should contribute to the state of the art and/or should be a good expository paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the paper is purely expository it should be clearly designated as such. Judge whether the substance is significant enough to warrant publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: All technical material must be accurate (e.g., no incorrect equations, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A referee should check technical correctness carefully and point out errors or ambiguities; offer references or corrections where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and readability (English/style)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article must be understandable, readable, and written in good English style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees should comment on exposition problems, ambiguous notation, or poor prose; suggest reorganization, clearer definitions, or stylistic edits to improve readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of bibliography
rubrics_metrics.description: The bibliography should be adequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for missing relevant references, incorrect citations, or insufficient literature context; suggest additional citations when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness / responsiveness of referees
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not postpone refereeing; return the manuscript promptly or decline immediately if unable to review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It takes no longer to review today than later; if you cannot referee, return it immediately. The refereeing cycle is on the publication critical path — respond quickly (text emphasizes not delaying and suggests a short expected turnaround).

rubrics_metrics.name: Report submission conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Return the manuscript to the editor; do not mark up the copy sent to the author; submit the report in duplicate; you may choose whether to include your name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If desired, write an accompanying letter to the editor (which will not be passed to the author) but that letter must not substitute for the referee's report. One copy of the report will be sent directly to the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of confidential letter to editor
rubrics_metrics.description: If you wish, write a separate private letter to the editor that will not be passed to the author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: That letter must not constitute the referee's report; keep the formal report separate and suitable for the author to receive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams: keep them small and focused
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrams are good if they are kept small; they should convey an impression or essential features without overwhelming the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fold-out or large diagrams can be useful if they capture essential structure (examples: fold-out syntax chart, performance comparison charts). Prefer diagrams that readers can quickly grasp; place explanatory text opposite the diagrams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams: include necessary detail but make details skippable
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed figures are acceptable if the additional detail is there for those who want it but can be ignored by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A figure may include fine-grained detail for expert readers while still allowing non-expert readers to get the main point. Example: a detailed prepaging figure whose fine lines can be ignored by casual readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer real (unchosen) test data to contrived examples
rubrics_metrics.description: When illustrating algorithms or phenomena, use real data rather than 'sample' data that have been cooked up solely as an example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Real test data (e.g., a paragraph from Grimm's Fairy Tales as line-breaking input) give more convincing illustrations; disclose if shown 'deliberate mistakes' so printers/reader don't 'correct' them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustration workload consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of work involved in preparing a paper for publication grows rapidly with the number of illustrations (jokingly proportional to the cube of the number of illustrations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit unnecessary illustrations; weigh the editorial/production cost of many figures and colors versus the clarity benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of color: talks vs papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Color can be used effectively in talks, but usually not in papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve multi-color illustrations for cases where they are essential; be mindful that color reproduction in print is costly or impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tables and numerical displays
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerical tables can present ideas that can't be demonstrated graphically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tables when they convey information better than diagrams; arrange text opposite diagrams and tables for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof exposition: minimize convoluted notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for notation that needs no double subscripts or subscripted superscripts; simplify notation where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recast proofs so the main idea remains but the presentation is shorter and clearer. The homework explicitly requires removing subscripted subscripts/superscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof exposition: prefer words and factoring to heavy notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use plain words instead of dense notation where they improve comprehension, and factor proofs into subgoals (describe subgoal then apply it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holding back on notation (introducing it only when needed), stating the proof technique (e.g., 'essentially a diagonalization technique'), and factoring the proof into parts reduce cognitive load for readers; graders found wordy/factored proofs easier to understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof exposition: handle special cases/initialization explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful about omitted initializations or special-case handling that can confuse readers; single out k=1 or similar base cases if it improves exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concede to readers unfamiliar with empty constraints by explicitly initializing where necessary; small concessions to clarity are worthwhile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use visual aids (histograms, scattergrams) judiciously to illustrate distributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use histograms and scattergrams to show frequency or multidimensional variation, but be aware of bias introduced by selecting/writing examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose biases (e.g., rewriting ugly paragraphs biases histograms); use visualizations to complement narrative, not to mislead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations: use sparingly and appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations can be used to open/close chapters when they express meaning better than the author can, or are beautiful or witty; avoid quotation solely to appear learned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search systematically (Bartlett, OED, concordances) for apt quotations; quoting oneself or out-of-context lines is acceptable when apt. Excessive or pretentious quotation bores readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing and typographic attention to detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide good indexes and attend to typographic details (e.g., paragraph indents, last-line lengths) to avoid odd page appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take indexing seriously (examples of historical suggestions); adjust wording when necessary so paragraph line-lengths and indentations do not make the page look strange.
